newsitem.title: USA: Securities are the gifts that keep on giving.
newsitem.headline: Securities are the gifts that keep on giving.

text.p: If you have nieces, nephews, grandchildren, or kids of your own that you'd like to get started on investing, you can buy them shares of a stock or mutual fund instead of a toy this holiday season.
That's always been an option for the wealthy, but this year there are more choices than before for relatives who want to be generous but don't have thousands to blow.

The best bet in financial gifts this year is individual stocks. When you give individual stocks, you're giving children the gift of something concrete: A company they can follow, shop at, and look up in the paper, according to Boston investment advisor Michael Hengehold.

There's been an enormous growth in direct stock purchase plans. These are programmes through which companies allow investors to buy one or more shares without paying any commissions or going through a broker. They differ from more traditional dividend reinvestment plans that require participants to already hold one share of stock.
Charles Carlson, a publisher who specialises in tracking these direct purchase plans, notes that some of the new entries are particularly child conscious:

Mattel sells for about $31 a share, and requires a $500 initial purchase, more than you'd spend on a Barbie but less than you could spend outfitting her with clothes, a car and a dream house. Then your young friend would own a piece of every Barbie that left the shelves. And you wouldn't have to worry about future birthdays and celebrations: More shares for every occasion could keep lots of kids interested.
Other direct-purchase stocks that may be kid pleasers, according to Carlson, include American Recreation Centres, Cadbury Schweppes, McDonald's, Proctor & Gamble, J.C. Penney and Wal-Mart.
To find direct purchase stocks, you can call the Direct Stock Purchase Plan Clearinghouse, run by Carlson in conjunction with a New York firm, Shareholder Communication Corp.
Call 1-800-774-4117 to get information and enrollment forms for more than 80 direct purchase stocks.

Many now cater to kids or their parents, but it still takes a fair amount of cash to get in the door. The most well-known, The Stein Roe Young Investor fund, has cut its minimum investment to $100 if you agree to make regular monthly investments; other funds offered by T. Rowe Price in Baltimore waive minimums altogether if you agree to invest just $50 a month.

The Twentieth Century Gifttrust is a fund designed specifically for accounts opened as gifts or transfers to minors: You have to agree to leave the money in for at least 10 years to even open an account there. But the fund is consistently at the top of the heap, notes Hengehold; that 10-year commitment gives the fund's managers some security that they can trade on.
The Mutual Fund Education Alliance, a trade group of no-load and inexpensive mutual funds, has a list of kid-smart funds (sponsored by the funds, don't forget) at its Web site: http://www.mfea.com.

If you want to invest for a child, you should check with his or her parents first. They may be investment phobic themselves and may not want to manage their child's account. Or they may be trying to keep their children free of assets to better qualify for financial aid during the college years.

But if you have close enough ties to the child to keep on contributing, you can really make a difference in their financial health. Start with a 5 year old, commit to $50 a month, and they can easily have $20,000 when they turn $21.

You can Email Linda Stern at 72160.1546(at)compuserve.com or write to her in care of Reuters, Suite 410, 1333 H St., NW, Washington, DC 20005. She regrets that she cannot answer each letter individually, but will cover your questions in upcoming columns.
(EDITORS: Linda Stern is a freelance writer who covers personal finance issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Ms. Stern.)
